points.title: Le passé simple : reconnaissance en lecture
points.explanationEn:
The passé simple is a simple (one-word) past tense that means exactly what the passé composé means — a completed action in the past — but it belongs to a completely different register. It survives almost exclusively in written narration: novels, short stories, historical writing, fairy tales, and formal biographical or journalistic prose. No French person uses it in conversation, and if you tried to say il alla à Paris out loud in casual speech, it would sound bizarre, like a costume drama. Your goal at this level is not to produce the passé simple — you will never need to conjugate it in speech or in an email — but to recognize it instantly when reading so that a sentence like 'Il se leva, prit son manteau et sortit sans un mot' doesn't slow you down or look like a typo of a verb you already know.

The formation splits into three families. -ER verbs take the endings -ai, -as, -a, -âmes, -âtes, -èrent: il parla (he spoke), ils mangèrent (they ate), elle regarda (she looked). Because the je/tu/il forms of -ER verbs look almost like the present tense minus a letter, they're usually easy to spot from context. Most -IR and -RE verbs, plus many irregulars, take -is, -is, -it, -îmes, -îtes, -irent: il finit (he finished — note this is IDENTICAL in spelling to the present tense il finit, so only context tells you which tense you're in), elle vendit (she sold), ils prirent (they took, from prendre), il dit (he said, from dire). A third group, mostly verbs whose past participle ends in -u, takes -us, -us, -ut, -ûmes, -ûtes, -urent: il fut (he was, from être), elle eut (she had, from avoir), ils voulurent (they wanted). A small handful of high-frequency irregulars are worth memorizing by sight rather than by rule, above all il fut and il eut, since être and avoir appear constantly as auxiliaries and existential markers in narrative prose, and their passé simple forms look nothing like their infinitives.

The key recognition strategy is this: when you hit a verb form with an unfamiliar-looking ending on a stem you otherwise recognize, and the sentence is clearly narrating a sequence of past events in a literary text, assume passé simple before assuming a typo or an unknown verb. The circumflex accents in the nous/vous forms (-âmes, -îmes, -ûmes) are a strong tell, as are third-person singular endings that don't match any present-tense pattern you know (-a, -it, -ut for il/elle/on). Third-person forms (il/elle/on and ils/elles) are by far the most important to recognize, since first- and second-person passé simple is vanishingly rare outside first-person literary memoir — narrators mostly write about 'he,' 'she,' and 'they.'

Closely paired with the passé simple in literary narration is the subjonctif imparfait (imperfect subjunctive) and its compound counterpart, the subjonctif plus-que-parfait. These are the literary-register subjunctive equivalents that appear where spoken French would simply use the present subjunctive or the past subjunctive. The imperfect subjunctive is built from the passé simple stem (the ils/elles form minus -èrent/-irent/-urent) plus a set of endings with a distinctive circumflex in the third-person singular: qu'il parlât, qu'elle finît, qu'il fût, qu'elle eût. That circumflexed third-person form is the single most recognizable signature of literary subjunctive — spotting an â, î, or û right before a final t in a subordinate clause after que is a strong signal you're looking at this tense, not a typo. The plus-que-parfait du subjonctif is simply the imperfect subjunctive of avoir or être plus a past participle: qu'il eût parlé, qu'elle fût partie — functioning exactly like the plus-que-parfait indicative but in subjunctive contexts, often after si (in highly literary conditional sentences) or after verbs/expressions of doubt, emotion, or necessity set in a past narrative frame.

examples.fr: Il naquit à Paris en 1802 et mourut à Rome en 1867.
examples.en: He was born in Paris in 1802 and died in Rome in 1867.
examples.note: naquit (naître) and mourut (mourir) are classic biographical passé simple forms

examples.fr: Elle ouvrit la porte, regarda dehors, puis la referma lentement.
examples.en: She opened the door, looked outside, then closed it again slowly.
examples.note: three -ir/-er verbs in sequence — a typical narrative chain

examples.fr: Ils comprirent alors que tout était perdu.
examples.en: They understood then that everything was lost.
examples.note: comprirent, from comprendre, is easy to confuse with a present-tense form at a glance

examples.fr: Ce fut le plus beau jour de sa vie.
examples.en: It was the most beautiful day of her life.
examples.note: fut (être) — extremely common in narration; nothing like the infinitive

examples.fr: Elle eut soudain envie de tout abandonner.
examples.en: She suddenly felt like giving up on everything.
examples.note: eut (avoir), often confused with the noun 'eu' or the participle

examples.fr: Je voulais qu'il vînt me voir avant son départ.
examples.en: I wanted him to come see me before his departure.
examples.note: vînt is the subjonctif imparfait of venir, third-person singular

examples.fr: Elle craignait qu'il ne fût déjà trop tard.
examples.en: She feared it might already be too late.
examples.note: fût, subjonctif imparfait of être — the circumflex on û is the giveaway

examples.en: It was necessary that she leave immediately.
examples.note: partît, subjonctif imparfait of partir; a spoken register would just say qu'elle parte

examples.fr: Quand bien même il eût su la vérité, il n'aurait rien changé.
examples.en: Even if he had known the truth, he would have changed nothing.
examples.note: eût su is the subjonctif plus-que-parfait, used here in place of a spoken 'aurait su'

examples.fr: Le roi mourut sans qu'aucun de ses fils fût présent.
examples.en: The king died without any of his sons being present.
examples.note: fût présent, subjonctif imparfait after sans que, set in a past narrative frame

commonMistakes: Trying to actively conjugate and use the passé simple in speech or in emails/texts, where it sounds theatrically stilted — this tense is for recognition, not production, at any register short of literary composition.

Confusing third-person singular -ir/-re passé simple forms (il finit, il vendit) with present-tense forms that are spelled identically or nearly identically, and misreading the timeframe of a whole passage as a result.
Not recognizing high-frequency irregular stems like fut, eut, fit, vint, tint as forms of être, avoir, faire, venir, tenir, because they look nothing like the infinitives.
Missing the circumflex accent on subjonctif imparfait third-person forms (qu'il fût, qu'elle parlât) and misreading them as some other tense, or assuming the accent is a typo.

Assuming any qu'il/qu'elle + verb with an unusual ending must be present subjunctive, and mistranslating the nuance or time-setting the literary imperfect/pluperfect subjunctive actually signals within past narration.
whyItTrips: English has no equivalent split between a 'spoken past tense' and a 'literary past tense' — English simple past ('he went,' 'she said') works identically in speech and in novels, so the very idea of a tense reserved for the page feels alien.

Many passé simple and imperfect-subjunctive forms are visually close to other tenses learners already know (present, passé composé, infinitive), so the brain's first instinct is to force a familiar reading rather than recognize a new pattern.

Because textbooks for lower levels skip these tenses entirely, C1 learners often encounter them for the first time inside real literature, with no scaffolding — the tenses feel like a wall of irregular vocabulary rather than a small, learnable pattern.
